docs.tiltable.component: `Tiltable` is the card tap. It draws nothing — it ANSWERS one question: turned to its next stop,
what ANGLE does the element rest at? The answer is pure data, so a test reads it without a renderer
and a saved game reopens at the right tilt.
```ts
import { node, Bounded, Surfaced, Transformable, Tiltable, tiltAngle, nextTilt } from "game-kit"
const card = node("card",
Bounded({ bounds: rect(1, 1.4) }),
Surfaced({ surface: "queen" }),
Transformable({}),
Tiltable({ stops: [0, 90], wrap: true }))
tiltAngle(card, 0)   // 0   — upright
tiltAngle(card, 1)   // 90  — tapped sideways
nextTilt(card, 1)    // 0   — a tap past the last stop wraps to the first
## Discrete stops, not a free spin
A tilt turns to one of a FEW angles — a card is upright or tapped, a standee stands at 0 / 120 /
240 — never to 37.4 degrees. That free angle already has a home: `Transformable.angle` takes any
number and composes down the chain. `Tiltable` is the discrete cousin, and it earns a place only
where the set of angles is FINITE. The atom requires `Transformable`, because the stop it picks is
written straight into `angle` — the tilt is a pose, resolved.
## Two fields
`stops` — the angles, in degrees clockwise, in tap order. `wrap` — whether a tap past the last
stop returns to the first (`true`, the card that taps and untaps) or rests on the last (`false`, a
dial that stops at its end). That is the whole atom.
## The stop is not stored here
WHICH stop the card rests on is RUNTIME state — it is tapped in the course of a game — so it is an
index passed to `tiltAngle` and `nextTilt`, never kept on the atom. `Tiltable` holds only what the
stops ARE, which is spec: it does not change from tap to tap, lives on the node, and crosses the
wire once. This is the same split `Flippable` makes between the back surface and `faceUp`.
## A tap never points nowhere
An index past the ends CLAMPS into the stop list rather than throwing or resolving to nothing: pull
it below zero and the card holds on the first stop, past the last and it holds on the last. And
`nextTilt` on a node with no `Tiltable`, or a single stop, does not move the index — there is
nothing to step through, so the runtime state is left exactly as it was.
docs.tiltable.tap: One card and a dial that taps it. `index` is the runtime stop — the only thing `tiltAngle` is told
beyond the node itself. Drag it and the card turns, because the resolver picked the next angle in
`stops`: there is no second code path anywhere that says «the card is tapped».
`stops` is the list of angles, written as degrees — `0, 90` is upright and tapped; try `0, 120,
240` for a three-way standee. `wrap` decides the end of the list: on, a tap past the last stop
returns to the first; off, it rests on the last.
Pull `index` past the end of the list and the card does not vanish — it holds on the last stop, the
same clamp the atom makes for any out-of-range tap.
